value.overview: The Black-and-white Owl (Strix nigrolineata) is a medium-sized tropical owl of the family Strigidae. It has a dark, finely barred body, a blackish facial disk edged with pale markings, and bright yellow-orange eyes, bill, and feet. This mostly nocturnal species inhabits humid forests and wooded landscapes from Mexico through Central America into northern South America. It is generally solitary and is often detected by its distinctive calls rather than by sight.
value.classification: The Black-and-white Owl belongs to the owl family Strigidae and the order Strigiformes. It has also been treated under the genus Ciccaba, so both Strix nigrolineata and Ciccaba nigrolineata may appear in references.
value.identification: Adults are about 35–40 cm long and have a strongly contrasting black-and-white appearance. The upperparts are mostly sooty black, while the breast, belly, and undertail are finely barred or streaked with white. A pale, barred collar surrounds the back of the neck, and the dark facial disk has whitish lines or spots around the eyes and bill. The eyes, bill, cere, and legs are yellowish to orange. It lacks ear tufts. Juveniles are paler and more brownish overall.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from central Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama, extending south through Colombia and western Ecuador to northern Peru and Venezuela. In Costa Rica it is a native, resident owl, generally uncommon to rare and local in the lowlands and foothills, from sea level to about 1,500 m in suitable areas. It uses humid primary and secondary forest, forest edges, gallery forest, evergreen woodland, and wet or seasonally dry forest, including some wooded areas near people.
value.migrationStatus: The Black-and-white Owl is considered non-migratory and occurs year-round in Costa Rica. Individuals may move locally in response to food, breeding, or habitat conditions, but there is no regular long-distance migration.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited. The species is believed to nest in natural tree cavities or other sheltered sites in large trees, and it may also use abandoned nests or cavity-like structures. In Costa Rica, breeding appears to occur mainly during the dry season, although timing can vary regionally. Clutches are small, as is typical of many forest owls, and both adults are expected to contribute to defense and care of the young. A juvenile has been observed with adults in Costa Rica in December.
value.dietFeeding: The Black-and-white Owl hunts mainly at night from perches in forest interiors, edges, and clearings. Its diet includes large insects and other arthropods, as well as small mammals, birds, frogs, lizards, and possibly other small vertebrates. It often watches from a concealed perch before making a short, direct attack. Small ponds, open ground, and forest margins may provide useful hunting areas where prey is easier to detect.
value.behavior: This owl is primarily nocturnal, solitary, and relatively secretive. During the day it usually roosts quietly in dense foliage, shaded branches, or forest subcanopy, where its dark plumage can provide camouflage. It becomes active after dusk and uses repeated calls to advertise territory or communicate with a mate. It may tolerate some human-modified surroundings when mature trees and nearby forest remain available, but it is most closely associated with wooded habitats.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified. Some regional declines may occur where mature forest is cleared, but the available global assessment does not place the species in a threatened category.
